lessons.title: Watch List — OSI Model
lessons.brief:
Before writing any code, it helps to know where HTTP lives. The OSI model splits network communication into seven layers; HTTP is an application-layer (layer 7) protocol, and it relies on everything below it.

  • 7 · Application — you are here. HTTP, DNS, TLS.
  • 6 · Presentation — encoding, compression, TLS records.
  • 5 · Session — connection state.
  • 4 · Transport — TCP/UDP. HTTP/1.1 rides on TCP: ordered, reliable bytes.
  • 3 · Network — IP addresses and routing between machines.
  • 1–2 · Link/Physical — Ethernet, Wi‑Fi, the wire.

When your Python or C# server binds a port and someone connects, TCP (layer 4) has already done the handshake and guaranteed the bytes arrive. Your job is purely layer 7: read the request text, decide what it means, and write a response.

Watch the OSI-model video for this lesson, then continue to HTTP — Protocol Introduction.
lessons.hints: Nothing to build in this lesson — it is context. Press Skip if you already know the layers.

lessons.title: HTTP — Protocol Introduction
lessons.brief:
HTTP is a text-based request/response protocol. The client writes a request, the server writes a response. Both look like this:

GET /health HTTP/1.1

Host: 127.0.0.1:8081

A request is request line (METHOD PATH VERSION), then zero or more headers (Name: value), then a blank line, then an optional body.

The response mirrors it: a status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers, a blank line, then the body. The status code carries the meaning: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx your fault, 5xx the server's fault.

Task: bring up a server that answers GET / with 200 and a small plain-text body, and GET /health with 200 and the body UP. Anything else should be 404.
lessons.hints:
Return Content-Type: text/plain so clients display the body as text.

Map paths explicitly; if no route matches, send 404 with a short message.

starters.python:
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a):  # keep the console clean
        pass

    def _text(self, code, body=""):
        self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body.encode())

    def do_GET(self):
        # TODO: route "/" and "/health"; 404 otherwise
        self._text(200, "OK")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8081), Handler).serve_forever()

lessons.title: HTTP — Create HTTP Server
lessons.brief:
Now make the server do something useful: parse the request and write a real response. Every framework hides the same three steps — read the method and path, decide the status code, write headers then body.

Watch two details that trip people up:

  • The path and query string are separate. /echo?msg=hi has path /echo and query msg=hi. Split on the first ?.
  • Never echo untrusted input without a status decision — a missing parameter is a client error, so it is 400, not 200.

Task: implement GET /ping → 200 body pong; GET /echo?msg=X → 200 body X; GET /echo with no msg → 400; unknown paths → 404.
lessons.hints:
Python: urllib.parse.urlparse splits self.path into .path and .query; parse_qs turns the query into a dict.

C#: ctx.Request.Url.AbsolutePath is the path; ctx.Request.QueryString["msg"] is the parameter.

Set Content-Length when you know the body size; it is good hygiene.

from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

    def _text(self, code, body=""):
        self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body.encode())))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body.encode())

    def do_GET(self):
        u = urlparse(self.path)
        # TODO: /ping, /echo, else 404
        self._text(404, "not found")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8081), Handler).serve_forever()

lessons.title: HTTP — Multi Paths & Querystring
lessons.brief:
A real server is a router: a table from (method, path) to a handler. The querystring is data, not identity — two requests to the same path with different queries hit the same handler.

Task: build a small router. GET / → 200 and an index listing available routes. GET /sum?a=2&b=3 → 200 body 5 (parse both as integers). If a or b is missing or not a number → 400. GET /routes → 200 and a comma-separated list /,/sum,/routes. Everything else → 404.
lessons.hints:
Parse integers defensively — a query value is always a string. Python: int(x) inside try/except ValueError. C#: int.TryParse.

Order matters: check a and b presence before converting.

lessons.title: HTTP — Basic Authorization
lessons.brief:
Basic auth puts credentials in a header: Authorization: Basic base64(user:password). The server decodes the base64, splits on the first :, and compares.

Three rules for a correct implementation:

  • Missing or bad credentials → 401 and a WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="..." header. Without the header, clients do not know how to authenticate.
  • Decode defensively: malformed base64 or a value with no : is a 401, never a crash.
  • The scheme is case-insensitive (basic is valid), and the method must match — POST /admin is 405, not 401.

Task: protect GET /admin with user nova and password duel. Valid → 200 body welcome, nova. Anything else → 401 with the challenge header.
lessons.hints:
Python: import base64; base64.b64decode(value, validate=True) raises on garbage — treat that as 401.

C#: Convert.FromBase64String throws FormatException; wrap it.

Split credentials on the first colon only: user:pass:extra has password pass:extra.

lessons.title: HTTP — Bearer Authorization (Token)
lessons.brief:
Bearer tokens replace passwords with an opaque string: Authorization: Bearer <token>. The server checks the token, not a username/password pair. "Bearer" means whoever holds it is granted access — which is why tokens are secret and short-lived.

Task: protect GET /data. Valid token nivix-secret → 200 with a JSON body {"ok":true} and Content-Type: application/json. Missing, wrong token, or the wrong scheme → 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer.

Compare tokens with a constant-time comparison when it matters (e.g. hmac.compare_digest / CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals) to avoid timing leaks.
lessons.hints:
Split the header into exactly two parts: scheme and credentials. More or fewer → 401.

The scheme comparison is case-insensitive; the token comparison is exact.

lessons.title: HTTP — Create HTTP Client
lessons.brief:
Servers are also clients. A proxy endpoint receives a request, makes an outbound request of its own, and returns the result. This is the heart of gateways, webhooks and API aggregators.

Task: implement GET /fetch?url=<url>. Your server should perform a GET to that URL and return the upstream status code and body. If url is missing → 400. If the outbound request fails → 502.

The judge will ask your server to fetch its own /ping, so a working server must be able to talk to itself.
lessons.hints:
Python: urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=5).read(). Catch URLError → 502.

C#: new HttpClient().GetStringAsync(url) inside a try/catch.

Never blindly trust the url parameter in production (SSRF) — here it is local, but say so in a comment.

lessons.title: HTTP — POST Request
lessons.brief:
POST carries a body. With a GET the meaning lives in the URL; with a POST the payload is in the body and its type is declared by Content-Type. If the server does not support the type it should say 415 Unsupported Media Type — not silently misparse it.

Task: implement POST /submit accepting application/json of the form {"name":"...","score":<int>} and answering 200 with {"ok":true,"score":<int>}. Rules: wrong/missing Content-Type → 415; body that is not valid JSON or is missing fields → 400; GET /submit → 405.

Read exactly Content-Length bytes — the body is a stream, not a line.
lessons.hints:
Python: self.headers.get("Content-Length"), then self.rfile.read(n), then json.loads; catch ValueError/KeyError → 400.

C#: read the request stream to ContentLength64 bytes; System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.Parse.

Check Content-Type starts with application/json before parsing.

starters.python:
import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

    def _json(self, code, obj):
        body = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def do_POST(self):
        # TODO: /submit
        self._json(404, {"error": "not found"})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8081), Handler).serve_forever()
